summary: Offers guidelines for authors and reviewers of standards-track documents that define YANG data models, the modeling language used with NETCONF. The aim is better interoperability and usability. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 8407.

eli5.summary: A checklist for people who write and check the blueprints that describe how network gear is configured, so the blueprints all look alike and work together.

questions: how to review a yang data model
subtitle: Best practices for writing YANG data models in standards documents.

tldr.problem: YANG data model documents in standards have no consistent structure or conventions, making them harder for authors and reviewers to develop interoperable and usable specifications.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides a comprehensive checklist of guidelines for authors and reviewers covering documentation structure, naming conventions, data types, namespace assignments, security considerations, and YANG language best practices.
tldr.outcome: YANG specifications became more consistent and interoperable, benefiting NETCONF-based network management. This was superseded by RFC 8407.

today: RFC 6087 is obsoleted by RFC 8407, which provides updated authoring guidelines for YANG data models reflecting experience and changes since 2011.

sections.title: Introduction to YANG Guidelines
sections.content:
YANG is a data modeling language used with the NETCONF protocol to manage network devices and configuration. YANG modules define the data structures, operations, and notification messages that a network device supports through NETCONF.

This document provides guidelines for Standards Track specifications that define YANG data models. Unlike the YANG language specification itself, which defines minimum requirements, these guidelines define a higher level of consistency required for published standards. Many YANG constructs are optional in the language, but using them consistently across standards improves interoperability and usability. The guidelines cover documentation structure, module naming, data types, namespace assignments, and security considerations.

The document is structured similarly to SMIv2 usage guidelines, providing authors and reviewers with a reference for what good YANG standards look like.
sections.eli5: YANG is the language network engineers use to describe what configuration data a device supports. This memo is a checklist of best practices so all YANG descriptions look and work the same way.

sections.title: Documentation and Structure Requirements
sections.content:
Every YANG standards document must include several required sections beyond the module definitions themselves:

Narrative sections must include an overview describing the scope, field of application, and relationship to other standards. The narrative should also describe how the module data is organized. If the module imports from other modules, the overview must explicitly note those dependencies.

Definitions section contains the YANG module code itself, written in standard YANG syntax from RFC 6020. A YIN syntax version may also be provided.

Module copyright must reference the latest IETF Trust Copyright statement. Each YANG module in a document is considered code and must be wrapped in <CODE BEGINS> and <CODE ENDS> tags with the module filename.

Security Considerations section is mandatory. It must identify writable data nodes that could cause harm if misused, readable nodes containing sensitive data, and harmful operations, then explain the risks for each. The section should follow the latest approved template available online.

IANA Considerations section must be present for all standards submissions. If the module defines a new XML namespace, a new YANG namespace registry entry must be requested from IANA. If extending an existing namespace via a submodule, the main module must be updated with the latest submodule revision.

Reference sections must have normative references for every module import or YANG reference statement, and corresponding normative references must match the actual versions used.
sections.eli5: A YANG document needs certain chapters: what the module is for, the module code itself, security risks, IANA things, and references. Each one has specific rules.

sections.title: YANG Module Conventions and Naming
sections.content:
Module naming should use a distinctive word or acronym (such as the protocol name) in the module name. If extending existing modules, reuse the same word or acronym rather than creating a new one. All published module names must be unique, guaranteed by IANA for RFCs. Once a module name is published in an RFC, it must not be reused even if the RFC becomes Historic.

Identifiers in published modules must be between 1 and 64 characters in length, including any identifier-arg-str token.

Module header statements must include organization, contact, description, and reference statements. The organization should identify the IETF working group for Standards Track modules. The contact must include working group web and mailing information. Revision statements must be present for each published version and must reference the RFC containing that revision.

Namespaces must be globally unique URIs. For published IETF modules, the namespace should follow the form urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:<module-name>. IANA assigns the final namespace value. Until IANA assignment, a proposed namespace URI must be provided.

Top-level data nodes should not be mandatory, as this would make the database invalid when the module first loads. There should generally be only one top-level data node in each module.
sections.eli5: Module names should be permanent and unique. Metadata in the module header (who wrote it, contact info, history) is required. Data at the top level shouldn't be mandatory.

sections.title: Data Modeling Best Practices
sections.content:
Default values should not be stated explicitly when they match common defaults like config true or mandatory false, as this clutters the module with noise.

Data types should be selected carefully. For string data with patterns, pattern statements should be present. For bounded strings, length statements must be included. For numeric data, range statements should be present if bounds differ from the built-in type. Signed numeric types should only be used when negative values are semantically valid. For enumeration and bits types, each enum or bit value should have a description statement.

Reusable type definitions should reuse existing types from standard modules like RFC 6021 rather than defining new ones. Type definitions should include description statements and units statements where applicable. If a significant number of types will be reused across modules, they should be in a separate module for easier reuse.

Data definitions (containers, leaves, lists, notifications, operations) must have description statements. External references must be noted. The anyxml construct should be avoided in favor of more specific data types. Referential integrity constraints should be expressed with XPath must statements when needed.

Conditional statements using if-feature and when should be documented carefully. If data is optional due to NETCONF capabilities, an if-feature statement should indicate this. Conditional requirements must be documented in the description or with when/if-feature statements.

XPath expressions should avoid position() and last() functions, preceding/following axes, and preceding-sibling/following-sibling axes unless the server maintains document order. Int64 and uint64 types should not be used in numeric expressions due to precision limitations.
sections.eli5: Choose the right data type. Don't repeat defaults. Describe each field and any special conditions for using it. Be careful with math on big numbers.

sections.title: Lifecycle Management and Operations
sections.content:
Lifecycle tracking ensures modules remain maintainable over time. The status statement must be present if its value is deprecated or obsolete. Module and namespace names must never be changed after publication. Revision-date substatements should be present in import and include statements when groupings are used. If submodules are used, the main module's revision date must be equal to or more recent than any included submodule.

Operation definitions (RPC statements) must have description statements referencing any external specifications. If an operation impacts system behavior, this must be mentioned. Operations potentially harmful to system behavior must be discussed in the Security Considerations section.

Notification definitions must have description and reference statements. Security considerations apply to notifications that expose sensitive information.

Module review checklist (in appendix) provides a systematic way for reviewers to verify compliance with these guidelines. A YANG module template is provided showing the recommended structure.
sections.eli5: Once a module is published, its name and namespace never change. Operations and notifications need clear descriptions and security warnings.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 6087 is an Informational document that served as the authoritative guidelines for YANG module standards from January 2011. It was later obsoleted by RFC 8407, which provides updated and more comprehensive guidance on YANG data model document structure and authoring conventions.
sections.eli5: This memo was the official guideline for YANG authors starting in 2011. A newer RFC (8407) updated the rules later.
